🌊 Tideline: forecasting sea-level rise and testing coastal defences with machine learning¶

Course: 21CEO310T – Global Warming and Climate Change (LLT / CLA-2) Topic: Sea-level rise and coastal protection. Model a rising water level and compare protective approaches such as mangroves, raised structures and embankments.

1. Problem statement¶

The global ocean has risen by about 23 cm since 1880, and the rise is speeding up. Most of India's coastal cities (Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Surat) sit only a few metres above high tide, and a storm surge on top of a higher sea turns rare floods into regular ones. Planners have three families of defence:

  • Green: mangrove belts that slow waves and surge, trap sediment and store carbon.
  • Grey: embankments and seawalls that block water up to their crest height.
  • Accommodate: raised (stilted) houses that let water pass underneath.

Aim: forecast sea level to 2100 with explainable machine learning trained on real tide-gauge and satellite data, then use the forecast to compare how well each defence protects a model coastal town, and at what cost.

2. Objectives¶

  1. Build a clean annual dataset (1880–2024) from CSIRO tide-gauge reconstructions, NOAA satellite altimetry, NASA GISS temperatures and the PSMSL Mumbai tide gauge.
  2. Train and compare Linear Regression, SVR and Random Forest with MAE, MSE, RMSE and R² on an unseen future test period (2000–2024).
  3. Project sea level to 2100 under three IPCC warming pathways and check the result against IPCC AR6.
  4. Simulate storm floods for a model coastal town under four defences and compare flooded homes, expected annual damage, cost-benefit ratio and carbon captured.

3. What is novel here¶

# Novelty Why it matters
1 Semi-empirical physics features. The Rahmstorf / Vermeer law says the rate of sea-level rise is proportional to warming, dH/dt = a(T − T₀) + b·dT/dt. We feed the models the integral of temperature Linear Regression on these features is the published physical model, so its coefficients can be checked against the literature
2 Physics-guided hybrid (backbone + SVR/RF residual) Fixes tree and kernel models' inability to extrapolate to record sea levels
3 Global → local. Mumbai's tide gauge is linked to the global mean to estimate local land motion Coastal defence is decided locally, not globally
4 Living vs static defences. Mangroves gain height with sediment and survive slow sea-level rise, but drown above about 7 mm/yr. Embankments fail suddenly when overtopped Shows when each option stops working, not just whether it works today
5 Full cost-benefit and blue carbon. Expected annual damage from a storm-surge return-period curve, net present value and mangrove CO₂ uptake Connects adaptation (Unit V) with mitigation

Syllabus: Unit II (sea-level rise, cyclones, Indian climate system), Unit III (shoreline change, ice and glacier loss), Unit IV (IPCC assessments), Unit V (adaptation: mangroves, sustainable development, carbon sequestration). Course outcomes: CO-2, CO-3, CO-5.

SOURCES = {
    "csiro": ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datasets/sea-level-rise/main/data/CSIRO_Recons_gmsl_yr_2019.csv",
              "csiro_recons_gmsl_yr_2019.csv"),
    "altimetry": ("https://www.star.nesdis.noaa.gov/socd/lsa/SeaLevelRise/slr/slr_sla_gbl_free_ref_90.csv",
                  "noaa_star_gmsl.csv"),
    "mumbai": ("https://psmsl.org/data/obtaining/rlr.annual.data/43.rlrdata", "psmsl_mumbai_43.rlrdata"),
    "temp": ("https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/tabledata_v4/GLB.Ts+dSST.csv", "gistemp_glb.csv"),
}

def fetch(key):
    url, fname = SOURCES[key]
    path = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, fname)
    if USE_LIVE_DATA:
        try:
            req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (Tideline student project)"})
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as r, open(path, "wb") as f:
                f.write(r.read())
            print(f"✔ downloaded {fname:30s} from {url.split('/')[2]}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"⚠ could not download {fname} ({e.__class__.__name__}); using local copy")
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"{path} missing - upload the bundled data/ folder")
    return path

paths = {k: fetch(k) for k in SOURCES}

def quality_row(src, var, raw, s, units):

    return {"Source": src, "Variable": var, "Units": units, "Raw rows": len(raw), "Raw columns": raw.shape[1],
            "First year": int(s2.index.min()), "Last year": int(s2.index.max()), "Valid years": len(s2),
            "Missing years": int(s.isna().sum()), "Min": round(s2.min(), 1), "Max": round(s2.max(), 1)}

quality = pd.DataFrame([

    quality_row("NOAA LSA", "GMSL satellite altimetry", raw_alt, alt, "mm (annual mean)"),
    quality_row("PSMSL", "Mumbai relative sea level", raw_mum, mumbai, "mm (RLR datum)"),
    quality_row("NASA GISS", "Global temperature", raw_temp, temp, "°C vs 1951–80"),
])

5.2 Building one sea-level record (1880–2024)¶

Tide gauges are the only record before 1993; satellites are more accurate after it. We use CSIRO up to 1992 and NOAA altimetry from 1993, shifting the altimetry by the mean difference over their 1993–2019 overlap so the two join without a jump. Everything is expressed relative to the 1995–2014 mean, the IPCC AR6 baseline.

In [4]:
overlap = alt.loc[1993:2019].index.intersection(csiro.index)
offset = (alt.loc[overlap] - csiro.loc[overlap, "gmsl"]).mean()
splice_rmse = np.sqrt(((alt.loc[overlap] - offset - csiro.loc[overlap, "gmsl"]) ** 2).mean())
gmsl = pd.concat([csiro.loc[:1992, "gmsl"], alt.loc[1993:] - offset]).rename("gmsl")
gmsl = gmsl - gmsl.loc[BASE[0]:BASE[1]].mean()
years = gmsl.index
df = pd.DataFrame({"gmsl": gmsl, "T": temp_pi.reindex(years)})
df["source"] = np.where(df.index <= 1992, "CSIRO tide gauges", "NOAA altimetry")
df["gmsl_unc"] = csiro["gmsl_unc"].reindex(years).fillna(csiro["gmsl_unc"].iloc[-1])
print(f"Altimetry–CSIRO offset {offset:.1f} mm, agreement over the overlap RMSE {splice_rmse:.1f} mm")
print(f"Spliced record: {len(df)} years ({years.min()}–{years.max()}), rise {df.gmsl.iloc[-1] - df.gmsl.iloc[0]:.0f} mm")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4.6))

                csiro.gmsl + csiro.gmsl_unc - (csiro.loc[BASE[0]:BASE[1], "gmsl"].mean()), color=BLUE, alpha=0.15, linewidth=0,
                label="CSIRO ±1σ")
ax.plot(df.index[df.index <= 1992], df.gmsl[df.index <= 1992], color=BLUE, label="CSIRO tide-gauge reconstruction")
ax.plot(df.index[df.index >= 1993], df.gmsl[df.index >= 1993], color=ORANGE, label="NOAA satellite altimetry")
ax.axhline(0, color=AXIS, linewidth=1)
ax.set_ylabel("mm relative to 1995–2014"); ax.set_title("Global mean sea level, 1880–2024")

6. Physics-informed features (the semi-empirical sea-level law)¶

Warmer water expands and warmer air melts glaciers and ice sheets. Rahmstorf (2007) found that the rate of global sea-level rise is proportional to how far temperature is above an equilibrium value T₀. Vermeer & Rahmstorf (2009) added a fast term for the rate of warming:

$$\frac{dH}{dt} = a\,(T - T_0) + b\,\frac{dT}{dt} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad H(t) = a\!\int T\,dt \; - \; a T_0\, t \; + \; b\,T \; + \; c$$

So if we give a regression the features ∫T dt (cumulative warming), year and T, the fitted coefficients are the physical parameters a, T₀ and b. We use a trailing 3-year mean of T (no look-ahead) to reduce noise.

In [5]:
df["T3"] = df["T"].rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean()
df["cumT"] = df["T3"].cumsum()                       # °C·yr since 1880
df["dTdt"] = df["T3"].diff().fillna(0)
df["year_c"] = df.index - 1950                       # centred year
df.to_csv(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "tideline_dataset.csv"))
print(f"Model-ready dataset: {df.shape[0]} rows × {df.shape[1]} columns")
df[["gmsl", "T", "T3", "cumT", "dTdt"]].describe().T

7. Modelling¶

  • Chronological split: train 1880–1999, test 2000–2024. The test years hold the fastest rise ever measured, above anything seen in training.
  • Hyper-parameters are tuned with TimeSeriesSplit(5) inside the training years only.
Strategy Inputs Idea
A. Pure ML year, T the textbook approach
B. Semi-empirical features ∫T dt, year, T Linear Regression = Vermeer–Rahmstorf law
C. Physics-guided hybrid B as a linear backbone, then SVR / RF learn the residual from T and dT/dt each part does what it is good at
In [7]:
TARGET = "gmsl"
RAW, PHYS, RESID = ["year_c", "T3"], ["cumT", "year_c", "T3"], ["T3", "dTdt"]
train, test = df.loc[:TRAIN_END], df.loc[TRAIN_END + 1:]
tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)

def tuned_svr(kernels=("linear", "rbf")):
    grid = {"svr__kernel": list(kernels), "svr__C": [1, 10, 100, 1000], "svr__epsilon": [1, 3, 6], "svr__gamma": ["scale", 0.3]}
    return GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVR()), grid, cv=tscv, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")

def tuned_rf(shallow=False):
    grid = ({"n_estimators": [300], "max_depth": [2, 3], "min_samples_leaf": [8, 15]} if shallow else
            {"n_estimators": [300], "max_depth": [None, 6], "min_samples_leaf": [1, 3]})
    return GridSearchCV(RandomForestRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1), grid, cv=tscv,
                        scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")

class PhysicsGuidedHybrid(BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin):
    """Semi-empirical linear backbone + an ML model for the residual (bounded inputs only)."""
    def __init__(self, residual_model=None, features=tuple(PHYS), residual_features=tuple(RESID)):
        self.residual_model, self.features, self.residual_features = residual_model, features, residual_features
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.backbone_ = LinearRegression().fit(X[list(self.features)], y)
        r = y - self.backbone_.predict(X[list(self.features)])
        self.residual_ = clone(self.residual_model).fit(X[list(self.residual_features)], r)
        return self
    def predict(self, X):
        return self.backbone_.predict(X[list(self.features)]) + self.residual_.predict(X[list(self.residual_features)])

EXPERIMENTS = {
    "A · Linear Regression": (LinearRegression(), RAW),
    "A · SVR": (tuned_svr(), RAW),
    "A · Random Forest": (tuned_rf(), RAW),
    "B · Linear Regression": (LinearRegression(), PHYS),
    "B · SVR": (tuned_svr(), PHYS),
    "B · Random Forest": (tuned_rf(), PHYS),
    "C · Hybrid + SVR": (PhysicsGuidedHybrid(tuned_svr(("rbf",))), PHYS + ["dTdt"]),
    "C · Hybrid + Random Forest": (PhysicsGuidedHybrid(tuned_rf(shallow=True)), PHYS + ["dTdt"]),
}

def metrics(y, p):
    mse = mean_squared_error(y, p)
    return {"MAE": mean_absolute_error(y, p), "MSE": mse, "RMSE": np.sqrt(mse), "R²": r2_score(y, p)}

fitted, rows = {}, []
for name, (model, feats) in EXPERIMENTS.items():
    model.fit(train[feats], train[TARGET])
    fitted[name] = model
    rows.append({"Model": name, **metrics(test[TARGET], model.predict(test[feats])),
                 "Train R²": r2_score(train[TARGET], model.predict(train[feats]))})
results = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Model")
results.to_csv(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "model_metrics_test.csv"))
print("Test period 2000–2024 (25 unseen years). Errors in mm.")
results.style.format("{:.3f}").background_gradient(subset=["R²"], cmap="Blues").highlight_min(subset=["MAE"], color="#cde2fb")

Reading the results. Pure Random Forest cannot predict a sea level higher than anything it saw in training, so it flatlines through the 2000s; RBF-SVR drifts back toward its training mean. The semi-empirical features fix this: once the integral of temperature is an input, even simple Linear Regression follows the acceleration, and the hybrid lets RF and SVR join in without needing to extrapolate.

7.1 Robustness checks¶

  • Random-split trap: shuffling the years before splitting puts each test year next to almost identical training years, and the score looks better than it really is.
  • Rolling-origin validation: retrain on everything before 1960, 1980 and 2000 and test on the following 20–25 years.
In [9]:
Xs_tr, Xs_te, ys_tr, ys_te = train_test_split(df[RAW], df[TARGET], test_size=0.2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
rf_shuffled = RandomForestRegressor(300, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(Xs_tr, ys_tr)
trap = pd.DataFrame({"Random split (leaky)": metrics(ys_te, rf_shuffled.predict(Xs_te)),
                     "Chronological split (honest)": results.loc["A · Random Forest", ["MAE", "MSE", "RMSE", "R²"]].to_dict()}).T

def frozen(m):
    if isinstance(m, GridSearchCV): return clone(m.best_estimator_)
    if isinstance(m, PhysicsGuidedHybrid): return PhysicsGuidedHybrid(frozen(m.residual_))
    return clone(m)

roll = []
for start, end in [(1960, 1979), (1980, 1999), (2000, 2024)]:
    tr, te = df.loc[:start - 1], df.loc[start:end]
    for name, (_, feats) in EXPERIMENTS.items():
        m = frozen(fitted[name]).fit(tr[feats], tr[TARGET])
        roll.append({"Model": name, "window": f"{start}–{end}", **metrics(te[TARGET], m.predict(te[feats]))})
rolling = pd.DataFrame(roll)
rolling_summary = rolling.pivot(index="Model", columns="window", values="MAE").loc[results.index]
rolling.to_csv(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "rolling_origin.csv"), index=False)
display(trap.style.format("{:.3f}"))
print("Rolling-origin MAE (mm) per test window:")
rolling_summary.style.format("{:.1f}")

8. Explainability: does the model recover the physics?¶

In [10]:
lr = fitted["B · Linear Regression"]
a, c_year, b = lr.coef_                     # features: cumT, year_c, T3
T0 = -c_year / a
print(f"a  (sensitivity of the rate)  = {a:.2f} mm/yr per °C   [Rahmstorf 2007: 3.4; Vermeer & Rahmstorf 2009: 5.6]")
print(f"T₀ (equilibrium temperature)  = {T0:+.2f} °C above 1880–1900  (sea level is stable when T = T₀)")
print(f"b  (fast term)                = {b:.1f} mm per °C           [Vermeer & Rahmstorf 2009: −49]")
rate_now = a * (df['T3'].iloc[-1] - T0)
rate_obs = np.polyfit(df.index[-10:], df.gmsl.iloc[-10:], 1)[0]
print(f"Model rate for {df.index[-1]}: {rate_now:.1f} mm/yr  |  observed 10-year trend: {rate_obs:.1f} mm/yr")

imp = {}
for name in ["A · Random Forest", "B · Linear Regression", "C · Hybrid + Random Forest"]:
    feats = EXPERIMENTS[name][1]
    pi = permutation_importance(fitted[name], test[feats], test[TARGET], n_repeats=30, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
                                scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")
    imp[name] = pd.Series(pi.importances_mean, index=feats)
importance = pd.DataFrame(imp).T.fillna(0)
importance.round(2)

T₀ (equilibrium temperature)  = -0.61 °C above 1880–1900  (sea level is stable when T = T₀)
b  (fast term)                = -2.0 mm per °C           [Vermeer & Rahmstorf 2009: −49]
Model rate for 2024: 4.0 mm/yr  |  observed 10-year trend: 3.7 mm/yr

T3 cumT dTdt year_c
A · Random Forest 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.00
B · Linear Regression -0.13 15.28 0.00 9.42
C · Hybrid + Random Forest -0.11 15.27 0.12 9.41

Interpretation. The fitted a gives the extra millimetres per year of rise for each extra degree of warming. It is of the same order as the published semi-empirical values (a little lower than Rahmstorf's 3.4), the difference coming from the newer data version and our smoothing. More importantly, the model's rate for today matches the satellites' measured trend almost exactly. T₀ says the sea would only stop rising if the planet cooled back to about that temperature: we are far above it, so the rise keeps accelerating. Permutation importance shows the semi-empirical models rely on ∫T dt, the accumulated heat. The pure Random Forest leans on year and so has nothing to say about years it has never seen.

9. Global → local: Mumbai¶

Coastal defences face relative sea level, which also includes land rising or sinking. Over the same years we compare Mumbai's tide-gauge trend with the global trend. Local sea level is modelled as RSL = GMSL + β·t, where β = local trend − global trend is the combined land-motion and regional offset. A free regression on both GMSL and year is also shown, but the two inputs are almost collinear, so its split between α and β is unstable.

In [11]:
mum = pd.DataFrame({"rsl": mumbai, "gmsl": df["gmsl"]}).dropna()
mum["year_c"] = mum.index - 2000
mum_trend = np.polyfit(mum.index, mum.rsl, 1)[0]
glob_trend = np.polyfit(mum.index, mum.gmsl, 1)[0]
alpha, beta = 1.0, mum_trend - glob_trend
free = LinearRegression().fit(mum[["gmsl", "year_c"]], mum["rsl"])
print(f"Mumbai long-term trend {mum_trend:.2f} mm/yr vs global {glob_trend:.2f} mm/yr over the same {len(mum)} years")
print(f"Local offset β = {beta:+.2f} mm/yr → Mumbai's relative rise runs slower than the global mean (land uplift / regional ocean)")
print(f"(free fit for comparison: α = {free.coef_[0]:.2f}, β = {free.coef_[1]:+.2f} mm/yr, R² = {free.score(mum[['gmsl','year_c']], mum.rsl):.2f}; unstable because GMSL ≈ linear in time)")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4))
ax.plot(mum.index, mum.rsl - mum.rsl.loc[1995:2014].mean(), color=AQUA, marker="o", markersize=3, linewidth=1.2, label="Mumbai tide gauge (PSMSL)")
ax.plot(df.index, df.gmsl, color=BLUE, label="Global mean")

10. Projections to 2100¶

Warming pathways follow IPCC AR6 best estimates relative to 1850–1900: SSP1-2.6 (strong mitigation, ~1.8 °C in 2100), SSP2-4.5 (current policies, ~2.7 °C) and SSP5-8.5 (high emissions, ~4.4 °C). The semi-empirical law turns each temperature path into a sea-level path, and a block bootstrap of the training years gives the uncertainty band. We then compare 2100 with IPCC AR6's process-based medians.

In [12]:
T_START = df["T3"].iloc[-1]
PATHWAYS = {"SSP1-2.6": ([2024, 2050, 2100], [T_START, 1.75, 1.8]),
            "SSP2-4.5": ([2024, 2050, 2100], [T_START, 2.0, 2.7]),
            "SSP5-8.5": ([2024, 2050, 2100], [T_START, 2.4, 4.4])}
AR6_2100 = {"SSP1-2.6": (0.44, 0.32, 0.62), "SSP2-4.5": (0.56, 0.44, 0.76), "SSP5-8.5": (0.77, 0.63, 1.01)}   # m, median & likely range
future = np.arange(df.index.max() + 1, 2101)

def extend(model_coefs, T_path):
    """Integrate the semi-empirical law forward year by year from the last observed state."""
    a_, c_, b_, icpt = model_coefs
    cum = df["cumT"].iloc[-1]; out = []
    for yr, T in zip(future, T_path):
        cum += T
        out.append(icpt + a_ * cum + c_ * (yr - 1950) + b_ * T)
    return np.array(out)

rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE)
BLOCK, N_BOOT = 10, 500
starts = np.arange(len(train) - BLOCK + 1)
boot = []
for _ in range(N_BOOT):
    idx = np.concatenate([np.arange(s, s + BLOCK) for s in rng.choice(starts, len(train) // BLOCK + 1)])[:len(train)]
    m = LinearRegression().fit(train[PHYS].iloc[idx], train[TARGET].iloc[idx])
    boot.append((*m.coef_, m.intercept_))
# re-fit on all years for the projection (the test confirmed the model; now use every observation)
lr_all = LinearRegression().fit(df[PHYS], df[TARGET])
coefs_all = (*lr_all.coef_, lr_all.intercept_)
last_obs = df[TARGET].iloc[-1]
jump = lr_all.predict(df[PHYS].iloc[[-1]])[0] - last_obs      # start the projection from the observed level

projections = {}
for name, (yrs, temps) in PATHWAYS.items():
    T_path = np.interp(future, yrs, temps)
    central = extend(coefs_all, T_path) - jump
    sims = np.array([extend(bc, T_path) for bc in boot])
    sims = sims - (sims[:, :1] - central[:1])                 # align every bootstrap path at 2025
    projections[name] = pd.DataFrame({"T": T_path, "gmsl": central, "lo": np.percentile(sims, 5, axis=0),
                                      "hi": np.percentile(sims, 95, axis=0)}, index=future)

summary = pd.DataFrame({n: {"T 2100 (°C)": p["T"].iloc[-1], "GMSL 2050 (m)": p.loc[2050, "gmsl"] / 1000,
                            "GMSL 2100 (m)": p.loc[2100, "gmsl"] / 1000, "90% low": p.loc[2100, "lo"] / 1000,
                            "90% high": p.loc[2100, "hi"] / 1000, "AR6 median 2100 (m)": AR6_2100[n][0],
                            "AR6 likely range": f"{AR6_2100[n][1]}–{AR6_2100[n][2]}",
                            "Rate 2100 (mm/yr)": p["gmsl"].diff().iloc[-1]} for n, p in projections.items()}).T
summary.to_csv(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "projections_2100.csv"))
summary

Interpretation. Trained only on observations, the model lands inside the IPCC AR6 likely range for the low and middle pathways. Under SSP5-8.5 it sits below the AR6 median: a law calibrated on the 20th century cannot know how fast the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets will speed up in a much warmer world. The IPCC warns that rises above 1 m by 2100 cannot be ruled out under high emissions, so for planning the AR6 range is the safer upper bound.

11. Coastal-defence simulator¶

11.1 The model town¶

A 1 km stretch of a low-lying west-coast Indian town. The ground rises from +2.5 m above today's mean sea level at the shoreline by 0.3 % inland. 1,200 homes sit 50–1,500 m from the shore.

Flood level during a storm = sea-level rise (global × Mumbai factor + land motion) + high tide (MHHW) + storm surge (Gumbel distribution of annual maxima) + wave set-up.

Defence How it is modelled Source of parameters
Mangrove belt (width W) Wave height decays as e^(−kW), k = 0.005 /m (≈40 % per 100 m). Surge reduced by 0.25 m per km. The belt survives while relative sea-level rise is below 7 mm/yr; above that its health declines by 5 %/yr McIvor et al. 2012; Saintilan et al. 2020
Embankment (crest Zc) Dry while water + wave run-up stays below the crest. Once overtopped, the town floods as if undefended standard overtopping threshold
Raised houses (plinth h = 1 m) Water still enters, but each home's flood depth is reduced by h elevation-in-place
Hybrid 300 m mangroves in front of a lower 3.8 m embankment green-grey defence

Damage uses the JRC global depth-damage curve for Asian residential buildings (Huizinga et al. 2017). Expected annual damage (EAD) integrates damage over the return-period curve. Costs are illustrative unit costs, chosen so green defences cost a fraction of grey ones, as found by Narayan et al. (2016). They are meant to be edited.

In [14]:
SIM = {
    "town": {"shore_elev": 2.5, "slope": 0.003, "homes": 1200, "home_zone": [50, 1500], "home_value_usd": 40000,
             "people_per_home": 4.5, "length_km": 1.0},
    "sea": {"mhhw": 1.7, "surge_mu": 0.6, "surge_beta": 0.25, "wave_hs": 1.2, "setup_factor": 0.4, "runup_factor": 0.3},
    "local": {"alpha": float(alpha), "beta_mm_yr": float(beta)},
    "mangrove": {"k_wave": 0.005, "surge_cut_per_km": 0.25, "drown_rate_mm_yr": 7.0, "decline_per_yr": 0.05,
                 "cost_usd_per_ha": 8000, "om_usd_per_ha_yr": 300, "co2_t_per_ha_yr": 6.4},
    "embankment": {"cost_usd_per_m_per_km": 3.0e6, "om_frac": 0.01},
    "raised": {"cost_usd_per_home": 9000},
    "finance": {"discount": 0.04, "start": 2025, "end": 2100},
    "ddf_depth": [0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], "ddf_frac": [0, 0.33, 0.49, 0.62, 0.72, 0.87, 0.93, 0.98, 1.0],
    "return_periods": [1.05, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000],
}
MEASURES = {
    "No defence": {},
    "Mangrove belt": {"mangrove_w": 400},
    "Embankment": {"crest": 4.5},
    "Raised houses": {"plinth": 1.0},
    "Hybrid (mangrove + low embankment)": {"mangrove_w": 300, "crest": 3.8},
}
S = SIM
rng_h = np.random.default_rng(7)
HOME_X = np.sort(rng_h.uniform(*S["town"]["home_zone"], S["town"]["homes"]))
HOME_Z = S["town"]["shore_elev"] + S["town"]["slope"] * HOME_X

def surge(T):
    return S["sea"]["surge_mu"] - S["sea"]["surge_beta"] * np.log(-np.log(1 - 1 / T))

def local_slr_m(gmsl_mm, year):
    """Relative sea level at the town (m above the 2024 level)."""
    base = S["local"]["alpha"] * gmsl.iloc[-1]
    return (S["local"]["alpha"] * gmsl_mm - base + S["local"]["beta_mm_yr"] * (year - 2024)) / 1000

def ddf(depth):
    return np.interp(depth, S["ddf_depth"], S["ddf_frac"])

def event(slr_m, T, m, health=1.0):
    """Flood outcome for one storm of return period T. Returns (still level, flooded mask, damage fraction per home)."""
    w = m.get("mangrove_w", 0) * health
    wave = S["sea"]["wave_hs"] * math.exp(-S["mangrove"]["k_wave"] * w)
    still = slr_m + S["sea"]["mhhw"] + surge(T) - S["mangrove"]["surge_cut_per_km"] * w / 1000
    level = still + S["sea"]["setup_factor"] * wave
    if "crest" in m and level + S["sea"]["runup_factor"] * wave <= m["crest"]:
        return level, np.zeros(len(HOME_X), bool), np.zeros(len(HOME_X))
    depth = np.clip(level - HOME_Z - m.get("plinth", 0), 0, None)
    return level, level > HOME_Z, ddf(depth)

def ead(slr_m, m, health=1.0):
    rp = np.array(S["return_periods"]); p = 1 / rp
    dmg = np.array([event(slr_m, T, m, health)[2].sum() * S["town"]["home_value_usd"] for T in rp])
    return float(np.trapz(dmg[::-1], p[::-1]) + dmg[0] * (1 - p[0]))    # include the most frequent events

def capex(m):
    c = 0.0
    if "mangrove_w" in m: c += m["mangrove_w"] * 1000 / 1e4 * S["mangrove"]["cost_usd_per_ha"] * S["town"]["length_km"]
    if "crest" in m: c += m["crest"] * S["embankment"]["cost_usd_per_m_per_km"] * S["town"]["length_km"]
    if "plinth" in m: c += S["raised"]["cost_usd_per_home"] * S["town"]["homes"]
    return c

def om(m):
    c = 0.0
    if "mangrove_w" in m: c += m["mangrove_w"] * 1000 / 1e4 * S["mangrove"]["om_usd_per_ha_yr"] * S["town"]["length_km"]
    if "crest" in m: c += S["embankment"]["om_frac"] * m["crest"] * S["embankment"]["cost_usd_per_m_per_km"] * S["town"]["length_km"]
    return c

def run(scenario, m):
    p = projections[scenario]
    yrs = np.arange(S["finance"]["start"], S["finance"]["end"] + 1)
    slr = np.array([local_slr_m(p.loc[y, "gmsl"], y) for y in yrs])
    rate = np.gradient(slr * 1000)
    health, h = [], 1.0
    for r in rate:
        if "mangrove_w" in m and r > S["mangrove"]["drown_rate_mm_yr"]:
            h = max(0.0, h - S["mangrove"]["decline_per_yr"])
        health.append(h)
    health = np.array(health)
    e = np.array([ead(s, m, hh) for s, hh in zip(slr, health)])
    flooded100 = np.array([event(s, 100, m, hh)[1].sum() for s, hh in zip(slr, health)])
    area_ha = m.get("mangrove_w", 0) * 1000 / 1e4 * S["town"]["length_km"]
    return pd.DataFrame({"slr_m": slr, "rate_mm_yr": rate, "health": health, "ead_usd": e,
                         "flooded_homes_100yr": flooded100, "co2_t": area_ha * S["mangrove"]["co2_t_per_ha_yr"] * health}, index=yrs)

runs = {(sc, mn): run(sc, m) for sc in projections for mn, m in MEASURES.items()}
disc = (1 + S["finance"]["discount"]) ** -(np.arange(S["finance"]["start"], S["finance"]["end"] + 1) - S["finance"]["start"])
table = []
for (sc, mn), r in runs.items():
    base = runs[(sc, "No defence")]
    m = MEASURES[mn]
    pv_benefit = float(((base.ead_usd - r.ead_usd) * disc).sum())
    pv_cost = capex(m) + float((om(m) * disc).sum())
    table.append({"Scenario": sc, "Defence": mn, "Homes flooded 1-in-100 (2050)": int(r.loc[2050, "flooded_homes_100yr"]),
                  "Homes flooded 1-in-100 (2100)": int(r.loc[2100, "flooded_homes_100yr"]),
                  "EAD 2100 (USD M)": r.loc[2100, "ead_usd"] / 1e6, "Capex (USD M)": capex(m) / 1e6,
                  "PV benefit (USD M)": pv_benefit / 1e6, "BCR": pv_benefit / pv_cost if pv_cost else np.nan,
                  "CO₂ captured 2025–2100 (kt)": r.co2_t.sum() / 1000,
                  "Mangrove health 2100": r.health.iloc[-1] if "mangrove_w" in m else np.nan})
comparison = pd.DataFrame(table)
comparison.to_csv(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "defence_comparison.csv"), index=False)
comparison[comparison.Scenario == "SSP2-4.5"].set_index("Defence").drop(columns="Scenario").style.format("{:.2f}", na_rep="—")

11.2 What the simulator shows¶

  • Embankments give complete protection until the day they are overtopped, then fail all at once. That is the cliff edge of grey defences: rising seas push a once-in-a-century overtopping towards a once-a-decade one.
  • Mangroves cost the least and capture carbon, but only cut wave and surge energy, so the deepest floods still arrive. Under high emissions the rate of rise passes 7 mm/yr and the belt starts to drown.
  • Raised houses do not reduce flooding; they reduce damage. They work well against frequent shallow floods and poorly against deep surge.
  • The hybrid is the most robust. Mangroves shave off the waves, so a lower and cheaper embankment holds for longer.

def clean(o):
    if isinstance(o, dict): return {str(k): clean(v) for k, v in o.items()}
    if isinstance(o, (list, tuple, np.ndarray, pd.Series, pd.Index)): return [clean(v) for v in list(o)]
    if isinstance(o, np.integer): return int(o)
    if isinstance(o, (float, np.floating)): return None if math.isnan(o) else round(float(o), 4)
    return o

13. Conclusions¶

  1. Data: six decades of satellites and fourteen decades of tide gauges were joined into one record (1880–2024) with a documented quality report and a measured splice error.
  2. Models: on the unseen 2000–2024 test period, pure Random Forest and RBF-SVR break down because sea level rises above anything they saw. Semi-empirical features and the physics-guided hybrid keep all three algorithms accurate (see the metric table for this run's MAE, MSE, RMSE and R²).
  3. Explainability: Linear Regression on the semi-empirical features recovers the physical constants of the Rahmstorf–Vermeer law, and its present-day rate matches the satellites.
  4. Projections: by 2100 sea level rises by several tenths of a metre even under strong mitigation, and the rate under high emissions is many times today's.
  5. Defences: no single defence works for every future. Grey defences fail suddenly, green ones fade slowly when the sea rises too fast, and raised homes only limit damage. A green-grey hybrid gives the best balance of protection, cost and carbon.

Limitations¶

  • The town, its costs and the surge statistics are illustrative, not a survey of a real ward.
  • The flood model is a static "bathtub" with wave and surge attenuation; it does not simulate water flowing inland over time.
  • Semi-empirical models assume the past relationship between warming and sea-level rise continues, and cannot represent sudden ice-sheet collapse.
